correctness.rationale: The source formula for G, its 1/2 geodesic Lipschitz norm, and the distributional support-function inversion were verified against An, Section 6.1, equations (7)--(11). Both explicitly specified measures are probabilities of zero first moment: (1-s)=sc. Their supports are not antipodal pairs for every 0<ε<π/2. The displayed nonnegative coupling has transportation cost s[cε+(1-c)(π/2-ε)]. Substitution of G(0), G(ε), G(π/2) yields the exact angular support difference 2πsEε. Eε/ε→1/2 and Tε/ε→1, so its Hausdorff/W1 quotient tends to π from below; the published universal π upper bound gives sharpness. Periodic heat convolution preserves vanishing first moment and yields positive C-infinity curvature densities; its weak convergence gives convergence of W1 and uniform Green convolutions, proving sharpness also among smooth strictly convex bodies. The actual standalone check.py regression was executed successfully; the limit argument is analytic, not finite testing. No equality at finite ε is claimed.

originality.rationale: The closest work An arXiv:2610.11814v1 explicitly states after Proposition 6.3 that the optimal Lipschitz constant in Proposition 6.1 is not determined. Its Proposition 6.1 already proves ≤π, and its Proposition 6.3 proves only sharpness of exponent 1 with ratio π/3 for a two-fold cosine density. Our exact balanced triangle--rectangle family produces limiting ratio π, thus adds a matching bound not implied by the previously reported family. Direct comparisons with quantitative Minkowski stability, random normals reconstruction, and classical Gauss--Minkowski probability theory reveal distinct distances, centering, or objectives. Residual historical/unindexed equivalence risk is retained.

value.rationale: The motivating primary paper leaves its exact global coefficient undetermined, despite explicitly proving a π upper bound and a π/3 example. Determining an exact natural inverse-geometric stability constant answers that stated gap. The family of nondegenerate triangles versus rectangles identifies a meaningful boundary of the cone of balanced surface-area measures; heat smoothing shows that a smooth strictly convex restriction alone does not improve the optimum. This is a complete sharp all-measure result with a geometric explanation and direct significance for error calibration, not a routine reformulation or arbitrary finite parameter.
